memory_verse.label: Bible Reference
memory_verse.text: When Sihon and all his army came out to meet us in battle at Jahaz, the Lord our God delivered him over to us and we struck him down, together with his sons and his whole army. At that time we took all his towns and completely destroyed them—men, women and children. We left no survivors. But the livestock and the plunder from the towns we had captured we carried off for ourselves. - Deut 2:32-35 (NIV)

devotion.label: Devotion
devotion.text:
The battle came, and God gave the victory. "The Lord our God delivered him over to us." This is difficult reading, describing the complete destruction of Sihon's people in the conquest. We must not soften it, and we must place it carefully in its setting. This was a specific act of divine judgment on the Amorites at a particular moment in redemptive history — a people whose wickedness had reached its full measure (Gen 15:16). It was not a general model for how God's people treat their enemies, and it is certainly not a pattern for the church.

Under the new covenant, Jesus explicitly taught His followers a different way — to love their enemies and pray for those who persecute them (Matt 5:44). His kingdom does not advance by the sword against people (John 18:36). So we do not read this passage as license for violence, but as a sobering window into God's justice against entrenched evil at a unique point in Israel's history.

What we can draw from this, keeping it in its context, is the seriousness of God's judgment on sin and the certainty of His faithfulness to His promise. God had said He would give Sihon into Israel's hands, and He did. His word did not fail. The victory came not by Israel's might but by God delivering the enemy over to them.

The deeper truth for us is that the God of perfect justice, who judged sin in these ancient events, has provided a way of mercy. At the cross, God's justice against sin and His love for sinners met perfectly. The judgment we deserved fell on Christ, so that we could be spared (Isa 53:5). When we read hard passages of judgment, let them drive us to gratitude for the mercy we have received in Jesus, and to sober reverence for the holy God who does all things well.

reflection.label: Reflection
reflection.text:
1. How do you handle the hard passages of judgment in Scripture honestly?
2. Why is it important to read these in their redemptive-historical setting, not as a model for today?
3. How does the cross show both God's justice and His mercy?

prayer.label: Prayer
prayer.text: Holy God, I do not always understand Your judgments, but I trust that You are just and good. Thank You that Your justice against my sin fell on Christ, so I could receive mercy. Help me to revere You and to walk in the way of love Jesus taught. Amen.
